# Lightning rod (`lightning_rod`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by static_electricity, wire_drawing
- Core idea: Lightning is a giant electric spark and takes the easiest path to earth. A metal rod standing a metre or two above the highest point of the building, joined without gaps to a thick conductor (a copper or iron rod or strap about as thick as a finger) that runs down the outside by the shortest way into permanently moist ground, carries the stroke past the building. The conductor and its earth termination must both carry the stroke: a long buried rod or plate in wet soil, well away from the foundations. Gutters, bell frames and other large metal parts should be joined to the conductor.
- Pitfalls:
  - Poor earthing or a broken or corroded joint increases the risk of a side flash into the building
  - Expecting a rod to discharge an entire cloud. A rod can intercept a nearby strike and conduct its current to earth
  - Repeating the kite or insulated-rod experiment in a thunderstorm; Richmann was killed doing this in St Petersburg in 1753
  - Thin wire, sharp bends or a conductor led through the inside of the house
  - Ringing church bells against storms; it kept killing bell-ringers and should stop
- History: americas: 1750 – Franklin proposes pointed rods; 1752 earthed protective rods on the Philadelphia Academy and Pennsylvania State House. Franklin published instructions late that year in Poor Richard's Almanack for 1753; europe: May 1752 – At Marly a demonstrator acting for Dalibard draws sparks from a storm cloud with Franklin's insulated rod; 1754 Prokop Diviš erects an earthed 'weather machine' in Moravia (independence from Franklin disputed); rods spread from the 1760s against religious and learned resistance
- Read:
  - Benjamin Franklin, Experiments and Observations on Electricity (1751)
  - E. Philip Krider, Benjamin Franklin and the First Lightning Conductors (2004)
  - J. L. Heilbron, Electricity in the 17th and 18th Centuries (1979)
